extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in Russian/Soviet humor and folklore
extracted.subtask_description: Describing and classifying Russian/Soviet anecdotal jokes (anekdoty): their defining features, recurring archetypes, common themes, linguistic devices, and genre-specific motifs and settings. Useful for folklorists, translators, humor analysts, and writers studying Russian humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: short fictional stories or dialogs with a punch line
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Russian jokes (анекдоты) are short fictional stories or dialogs with a punch line, which commonly appear in Russian humor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically concise, delivered as a story or dialog culminating in a twist or one-line punch; central defining feature of the genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed categories with fixed settings and characters
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Russian joke culture includes a series of categories with fixed settings and characters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many jokes rely on recurring archetypes and set situations (e.g., military, village, office, exam, prison) so recognition of characters and setting is part of the humor; knowing archetypes helps both telling and interpreting jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical focus: sex, politics, family, and Soviet/Russian-specific subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes 'treat topics found everywhere in the world, including sex, politics, spousal relations, or mothers-in-law' but also discuss subjects particular to Russian or Soviet culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect Soviet-era institutions, bureaucracy, five-year plans, Chernobyl, Lenin/Politburo, anti-alcohol campaigns, and other culturally specific referents to be sources of punchlines; topicality often anchors the joke's meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language-dependent humor: untranslatability, puns, wordplay, and mat
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Every category has numerous untranslatable jokes that rely on linguistic puns, wordplay, and the Russian language vocabulary of foul language. (L) marks jokes whose humor value critically depends on intrinsic features of the Russian language.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many anecdotes exploit Russian morphology, affixation, homophony, and taboo words (mat); translators must note that literal translation often destroys the joke and cultural notes or adaptation are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of obscene vocabulary (mat) as a stylistic device
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The very use of obscene Russian vocabulary, called mat, can enhance the humorous effect... The taboo status often makes mat itself the subject of a joke.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mat can be used for emotional impact, lexical substitution, derivational play, or as a punchline contrast (e.g., genteel phrasing after an expected expletive); sensitivity to register and audience is crucial; some archetypes avoid heavy mat deliberately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and delivery: two-liners, dialogues, spoofs and parodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Many jokes are 'two-liners spoofing the solemn style of the original TV voice-overs' (example: Stierlitz) or short dialog exchanges (teacher/student, doctor/patient).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brevity and timing are central; parodic imitation of a solemn or authoritative voice (e.g., news, narration) is a common technique; meta-jokes and anti-climax endings are frequent devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-anchored humor: archetypes (Stierlitz, Poruchik Rzhevsky, Rabinovich, Vovochka, Chapayev/Petka/Anka)
rubrics_metrics.description: Named recurring characters function as compressed comic personas: e.g., Stierlitz (solemn spy parodies), Poruchik Rzhevsky (vulgar hussar officer), Rabinovich (Jewish protagonist), Vovochka (Little Johnny), Vasily Ivanovich/Chapayev (Red Army commander).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each archetype brings expected speech patterns, register, and joke conventions; successful jokes exploit or subvert these expectations; catchphrases and stock responses are common.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catchphrases and clichés as comedic currency
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain lines or phrases ('Gusary deneg ne berut!', 'Гусары, молчать!') become catchphrases within joke cycles and contribute to humor recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition and recognition of stock phrases add communal value and allow for meta-humor; catchphrases may be deployed as punchlines or signals of a joke type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intertextual parody: borrowing literary/film characters for contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes often use well-known literary or cinematic figures (Sherlock Holmes/Watson, Fantômas, characters from War and Peace) to create contrast, mimicry, or grotesque reinterpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarity with the source texts/performances enhances the joke; parodic imitation of voice or mannerisms (e.g., 'Элементарно, Ватсон!') is a frequent technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal fable structure and moral/pithy maxim punchlines
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Animals in Russian jokes are ... sapient beings with stereotypical behavior' and many animal jokes function as fables whose punchline is a maxim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anthropomorphic animal characters embody social or political types; expect concise moral-like punchlines and proverb-style endings; gendering of animals in Russian grammar plays into character roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folk-tale motifs (Golden Fish/Genie) with twist-based endings
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional motifs (e.g., the Golden Fish granting wishes) are adapted so the third wish becomes the punchline, often exposing greed or stupidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of folk motifs allows cultural shorthand; punchlines commonly invert the expected wish-fulfillment outcome, revealing character flaws or national stereotypes (e.g., vodka/three-person drinking).

rubrics_metrics.name: Drunkard jokes as a stable subgenre
rubrics_metrics.description: Drunkards are recurring protagonists; jokes exploit drunken logic, bravado, and absurdity (examples: urinating by a lamp post, anti-alcohol campaign code-talk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor arises from misapplied reasoning, malapropisms, and social commentary about alcohol culture; timing and bodily comic image important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policemen jokes: corruption and low intelligence themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Policemen (militsioners) jokes 'revolve around the supposition that the vast majority accept bribes' and often depict them as not very bright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect jokes about portable stop signs, petty corruption, and comic incompetence; jokes serve as social critique of law enforcement/bureaucracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethnic-stereotype categories and their melodic/phonetic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Many joke cycles target ethnic groups (Chukchi, Ukrainians, Georgians, Estonians, Finns, Jews, Chinese) using perceived traits, accents, and characteristic lexical/phonetic patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These jokes rely on stereotypical accents, structural sentence quirks, and cultural tropes; they distinguish between self-deprecating in-group variants (e.g., Jewish/Odesa humor) and out-group mockery; careful contextualization necessary due to potential offensiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chukchi jokes: 'primitive but clever' stereotype and one-word/stereotyped reply patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Chukchi are depicted as simple-minded yet shrewd; staple devices include repetition of 'odnako' and terse folkloric retorts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor often depends on contrast between geologist straight-man and Chukcha replies; use of formulaic short retorts and inversion of expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ukrainian jokes: rustic, stingy, food (salo) tropes and accent imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ukrainians are portrayed as rustic and fond of salo; accent and food preferences are comedic hooks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect parodies of accent, food-based punchlines, and jokes about perceived relations with Russians; cultural sensitivity advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgian jokes: theatrical accent, greed/sex tropes, and 'rich' stereotype
rubrics_metrics.description: Georgians are depicted with a loud theatrical accent and sometimes as wealthy or sex-obsessed; grammatical errors and Georgian words are imitated for effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jokes emphasize melodrama and wordplay between 'face' (лицо) and 'person' in Russian bureaucracy; rely on mimicry of accent and mannerisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estonian and Finnish jokes: slow, taciturn, and literal-minded archetypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Estonians and Finns are depicted as humorless, stubborn, taciturn, and slow; humor uses long vowels and repetition to suggest slowness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedic effect produced by drawn-out speech patterns and deadpan responses; often paired with ironic escalation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jewish/Odesa humor: self-deprecation, wit, and linguistic calques
rubrics_metrics.description: Jewish jokes in Russian culture are often self-deprecating, cynical, and witty, employing a Jewish accent and calqued sentence structures from Yiddish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These jokes rely on timing, rhetorical question-answer patterns, and community-specific frames; they are distinct from anti-Semitic jokes and often performed by Jews themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chinese-targeted jokes: population/linguistic-pun motifs and provocative mock-names
rubrics_metrics.description: Many jokes about Chinese exploit perceptions of population size, industriousness, and the visual similarity of pinyin syllables to obscene Russian words, producing mock-names/puns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linguistic similarity is used for wordplay (sometimes embarrassing diplomatic faux pas historically); translators must be sensitive to homophony-based humor and its offensiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-deprecating 'Russian' role in multi-national jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: When a Russian appears with Westerners, he often plays the simple-minded but ultimately resourceful figure — self-irony that reinforces national identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punchlines often reverse expectations (brute force triumphs over tech/skill) and serve as national self-image reinforcement; useful for studying cultural self-representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-Soviet 'vicious nineties' jokes: new-wealth and bandit themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes from the 1990s focus on oligarchs, New Russians, poverty, banditism, and the chaotic transition to 'jungle capitalism'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect satire of corruption, criminality as normal, and dark humor; these reflect socio-economic upheaval and are temporally specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chernobyl and disaster humor: taboo/black comedy about catastrophe
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes about Chernobyl and nuclear disaster use black humor to satirize official reports, radiation consequences, and bureaucratic absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an example of gallows humor; it mixes social critique with shock value and presumes audience familiarity with the event and its cover-ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical jokes: short doctor/patient dialogues and literalist misunderstandings
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical jokes commonly are short dialogs where literal interpretation, bureaucratic procedure, or absurd diagnoses produce punchlines (e.g., 'autopsy revealed cause of death was the autopsy').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic effect often derives from procedural literalism, dark irony, or institutional incompetence; timing and matter-of-fact delivery are key.

rubrics_metrics.name: University student jokes: scarcity, exams, khalyava and dorm-life motifs
rubrics_metrics.description: Student jokes lampoon cramped dorms, bad food, exam bilet rituals, last-minute cramming (khalyava), drinking, and stipend-related scarcity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jokes exploit academic rituals like random exam tickets, the social economy of students, and inventive evasion of duties; recognition of Soviet-era university life enhances comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cowboy and imported-genre jokes: cultural translation and dubbing parody
rubrics_metrics.description: Cowboy jokes in Russian often parody exaggerated Texan stereotypes or are shaped by poor dubbing of American films (voice-over mismatches), producing non-sequiturs and profanity jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These display how foreign genres are reinterpreted in Russian contexts; timing and juxtaposition with Russian idioms drive the comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disabilities and mental-hospital jokes: institutional satire and political subtext
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes set in asylums or about dystrophic patients often carry political subtext, satirize institutions, or deploy cruel irony about survival/health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often dark and potentially offensive; humor arises from inversion of expectations about sanity, survival, and bureaucratic absurdity; contextualize historically (Gulag references etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Taboo vocabulary as subject and mechanism of jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The taboo status often makes mat itself the subject of a joke' and the morphological richness of mat affords many derivations and substitutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors use polite or clinical phrasing as an ironic contrast to expected profanity, or exploit derivational morphology for comic creativity; audience and broadcast constraints affect use.
